prompt: Which of the following best describes the short-run Phillips curve (SRPC)?

options.label: A
options.text: A vertical curve showing unemployment fixed at the natural rate in every period

options.label: B
options.text: A downward-sloping curve showing a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: An upward-sloping curve showing inflation and unemployment rising together after demand changes

options.label: D
options.text: A horizontal curve showing inflation fixed regardless of the unemployment rate

options.label: E
options.text: A downward-sloping curve showing a long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment

explanation: The SRPC slopes downward because, in the short run, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation. The relationship is a short-run trade-off, not a permanent long-run relationship.

prompt: On a standard Phillips curve graph, the vertical and horizontal axes are labeled, respectively,

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment rate and inflation rate

options.label: B
options.text: Price level and real GDP

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP and inflation rate

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation rate and unemployment rate

options.label: E
options.text: Nominal interest rate and unemployment rate

explanation: The Phillips curve places the inflation rate on the vertical axis and the unemployment rate on the horizontal axis. This labeling allows the model to represent combinations of inflation and unemployment directly.

prompt: The downward slope of the SRPC indicates that, in the short run,

options.label: A
options.text: Higher inflation is associated with lower unemployment, and lower inflation is associated with higher unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: Higher inflation is associated with higher unemployment, and lower inflation with lower unemployment, holding other Phillips curve conditions constant

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment remains at the natural rate regardless of the inflation rate

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation remains unchanged as the unemployment rate varies

options.label: E
options.text: Inflation and unemployment are unrelated unless the natural rate changes

explanation: A downward-sloping SRPC represents an inverse short-run relationship between inflation and unemployment. Moving up and left along the curve means higher inflation and lower unemployment, while moving down and right means lower inflation and higher unemployment.

prompt: Which of the following is true of an economy represented by the Phillips curve model?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy operates on the LRPC only when unemployment is above the natural rate

options.label: B
options.text: The economy leaves the Phillips curve whenever a supply shock occurs

options.label: C
options.text: The economy can operate between SRPCs without being located on either curve

options.label: D
options.text: The economy is located on the SRPC only when inflation is positive

options.label: E
options.text: At any point in time, the economy operates somewhere along a short-run Phillips curve

explanation: The CED states that the economy is always operating somewhere along an SRPC. A supply shock can shift the SRPC, but the economy is still represented by a point on the relevant short-run curve.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the long-run Phillips curve (LRPC)?

options.label: A
options.text: A downward-sloping curve through the origin

options.label: B
options.text: An upward-sloping curve at the natural rate of inflation

options.label: C
options.text: A vertical curve at the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: A horizontal curve at the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: E
options.text: A vertical curve at the current inflation rate

explanation: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment. Its vertical shape means that the long run does not contain a stable trade-off in which permanently higher inflation produces permanently lower unemployment.

prompt: The unemployment rate represented by the vertical LRPC is the

options.label: A
options.text: Natural rate of unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: Current cyclical unemployment rate

options.label: C
options.text: Highest unemployment rate observed in a recession

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment rate associated with zero inflation

options.label: E
options.text: Lowest unemployment rate attainable in the short run

explanation: The LRPC is drawn at the natural rate of unemployment.

prompt: Long-run equilibrium in the Phillips curve model occurs at

options.label: A
options.text: The lowest point on the SRPC

options.label: B
options.text: The highest point on the SRPC

options.label: C
options.text: The intersection of the SRPC and the LRPC

options.label: D
options.text: Any point on the LRPC regardless of the SRPC

options.label: E
options.text: Any point at which inflation equals zero

explanation: Long-run equilibrium is the point where the economy's SRPC intersects the vertical LRPC. At that point, unemployment equals the natural rate and the economy is simultaneously represented on both curves.

prompt: A point to the left of long-run equilibrium on a Phillips curve graph represents

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: An inflationary gap because unemployment is above the natural rate

options.label: C
options.text: A recessionary gap because inflation is above its long-run value

options.label: D
options.text: Long-run equilibrium because inflation is positive

options.label: E
options.text: An inflationary gap because unemployment is below the natural rate

explanation: Points left of the LRPC have unemployment below the natural rate.

prompt: A point to the right of long-run equilibrium on a Phillips curve graph represents

options.label: A
options.text: An inflationary gap because unemployment is above the natural rate

options.label: B
options.text: A recessionary gap because unemployment is above the natural rate

options.label: C
options.text: A recessionary gap because unemployment is below the natural rate

options.label: D
options.text: An inflationary gap because inflation is below its long-run value

options.label: E
options.text: Long-run equilibrium because unemployment is positive

explanation: Points right of the LRPC have unemployment above the natural rate.

prompt: A change in aggregate demand will most likely be represented in the Phillips curve model by

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: E
options.text: A rotation of the LRPC around the natural rate

explanation: Demand shocks correspond to movements along a given SRPC.

prompt: A short-run aggregate supply shock will most likely be represented in the Phillips curve model by

options.label: A

options.label: B

explanation: Supply shocks correspond to shifts of the SRPC.

prompt: If the natural rate of unemployment increases, which curve must shift?

options.label: B
options.text: The LRPC shifts to the right

options.label: C
options.text: The SRPC shifts to the right

options.label: D
options.text: The SRPC shifts to the left

options.label: E
options.text: Neither curve shifts because the natural rate is fixed

explanation: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

prompt: If aggregate demand increases and there is no supply shock, the economy will most likely move

options.label: A
options.text: Down and to the right along the SRPC, toward lower inflation and higher unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: To a new SRPC to the right, with higher inflation and higher unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: Up and to the left along the SRPC, toward higher inflation and lower unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: To a new SRPC to the left, with lower inflation and lower unemployment

options.label: E
options.text: Vertically along the LRPC, with unchanged unemployment

explanation: A positive demand shock raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run. Because demand shocks produce movements along the SRPC, the economy moves up and left on the existing curve.

prompt: If aggregate demand decreases and there is no supply shock, the economy will most likely move

options.label: A
options.text: Down and to the right along the SRPC, toward lower inflation and higher unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: Up and to the left along the SRPC, toward higher inflation and lower unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: To a new SRPC to the right, with higher inflation and higher unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: To a new SRPC to the left, with lower inflation and lower unemployment

options.label: E
options.text: Vertically along the LRPC, with unchanged unemployment

explanation: A negative demand shock lowers inflation and raises unemployment in the short run. Since demand shocks correspond to movements along the SRPC, the economy moves down and right on the same curve.

prompt: An adverse supply shock that raises inflation and unemployment will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Shift the SRPC to the left

options.label: B
options.text: Move the economy up and left along the same SRPC

options.label: C
options.text: Move the economy down and right along the same SRPC

options.label: D
options.text: Shift the LRPC to the left without changing the SRPC

options.label: E
options.text: Shift the SRPC to the right

explanation: An adverse supply shock produces a less favorable inflation-unemployment combination, with both variables higher. In the Phillips curve model this is represented by a rightward shift of the SRPC.

prompt: A favorable supply shock that lowers inflation and unemployment will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Shift the SRPC to the right

options.label: B
options.text: Move the economy down and right along the same SRPC

options.label: C
options.text: Move the economy up and left along the same SRPC

options.label: D
options.text: Shift the LRPC to the right without changing the SRPC

options.label: E
options.text: Shift the SRPC to the left

explanation: A favorable supply shock allows lower inflation to coexist with lower unemployment.

prompt: Why does the Phillips curve model not imply a permanent long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: The SRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: The LRPC slopes downward only during recessions

options.label: C
options.text: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: The SRPC shifts whenever aggregate demand changes

options.label: E
options.text: The natural rate equals zero in the long run

explanation: The vertical LRPC shows that the long-run unemployment rate is the natural rate regardless of the inflation rate. Thus, different inflation rates can occur at the same long-run unemployment rate.

options.label: E

explanation: Because the LRPC is vertical at the natural rate, any point with unemployment equal to that rate lies on the LRPC. If the point is the economy's actual position, it is also on the relevant SRPC.

prompt: The natural rate of unemployment rises from 4 percent to 6 percent. Actual unemployment remains at 5 percent. How does the economy's gap classification change?

options.text: It changes from an inflationary gap to a recessionary gap

options.label: B
options.text: It remains an inflationary gap because actual unemployment is unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: It changes from a recessionary gap to an inflationary gap

options.label: D
options.text: It remains a recessionary gap because actual unemployment is unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: It becomes long-run equilibrium because 5 percent lies between the two natural rates

explanation: At a 4 percent natural rate, 5 percent actual unemployment is to the right of the LRPC and recessionary. After the natural rate rises to 6 percent, the same actual unemployment lies to the left of the new LRPC and is inflationary.

prompt: An adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC right, and aggregate demand then decreases. Which variable is certain to increase relative to its initial value if both changes are sufficiently small but nonzero?

options.label: A
options.text: Inflation

options.label: B
options.text: The natural rate of unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: The slope of the LRPC

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment

options.label: E
options.text: The natural rate and inflation together

explanation: The adverse supply shock raises unemployment, and the subsequent demand decrease also raises unemployment. Their effects on inflation oppose each other, but their unemployment effects reinforce one another.

prompt: A favorable supply shock shifts the SRPC left, and aggregate demand then increases. Which variable is certain to decrease relative to its initial value if both changes are nonzero?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: Inflation

options.label: C
options.text: The natural rate of unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: The slope of the LRPC

options.label: E
options.text: The inflation rate and natural rate together

explanation: A favorable supply shock lowers unemployment, and a subsequent positive demand shock lowers unemployment further. Inflation may rise or fall depending on relative magnitudes, but unemployment falls under both forces.

prompt: An adverse supply shock occurs while aggregate demand also increases. Which statement about the SRPC is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The SRPC shifts left because of the demand increase, and the supply shock moves the economy down-right along it, assuming no separate change in the other Phillips curve

options.label: B
options.text: The SRPC shifts right because of the supply shock, and the demand increase moves the economy up-left along the shifted SRPC

options.label: C
options.text: The SRPC remains fixed because the two changes offset, and only the LRPC moves

options.label: D
options.text: The demand increase shifts the LRPC right, while the supply shock shifts it left

options.label: E
options.text: Both changes are movements along the original SRPC, so no curve shifts

explanation: The supply shock determines the SRPC shift, moving it right. Once the new SRPC is established, the demand increase is represented as an up-left movement along that shifted curve.

prompt: A favorable supply shock occurs while aggregate demand also decreases. Which statement about the SRPC is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The SRPC shifts right because of the demand decrease, and the supply shock moves the economy up-left along it, with the natural rate otherwise unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: The SRPC remains fixed because the two changes offset, and only the LRPC moves

options.label: C
options.text: The demand decrease shifts the LRPC left, while the supply shock shifts it right

options.label: D
options.text: Both changes are movements along the original SRPC, so no curve shifts

options.label: E
options.text: The SRPC shifts left because of the supply shock, and the demand decrease moves the economy down-right along the shifted SRPC

explanation: The favorable supply shock shifts the SRPC left. The later demand decrease then moves the economy down-right along the new curve rather than shifting it again.

prompt: An economy starts in long-run equilibrium at 5 percent unemployment. A positive demand shock lowers unemployment to 4 percent. Before any other change, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy is in a recessionary gap and the SRPC has shifted right

options.text: The economy remains in long-run equilibrium because inflation increased

options.text: The LRPC shifts left to 4 percent unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: The economy is in an inflationary gap because the SRPC shifted left

options.label: E
options.text: The economy is in an inflationary gap and remains on the same SRPC

explanation: The demand shock moves the economy along the unchanged SRPC to unemployment below the 5 percent natural rate. A point left of the LRPC represents an inflationary gap.

prompt: An economy starts in long-run equilibrium at 5 percent unemployment. A negative demand shock raises unemployment to 7 percent. Before any other change, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy is in an inflationary gap and the SRPC has shifted left

options.label: B
options.text: The economy remains in long-run equilibrium because inflation decreased

options.label: C
options.text: The economy is in a recessionary gap and remains on the same SRPC

options.label: D
options.text: The LRPC shifts right to 7 percent unemployment

options.label: E
options.text: The economy is in a recessionary gap because the SRPC shifted right

explanation: The negative demand shock moves the economy down-right along its existing SRPC to unemployment above the natural rate. That location is a recessionary gap.

prompt: Which statement is most accurate when the natural rate changes but the current inflation rate and actual unemployment rate do not immediately change?

options.label: A
options.text: The SRPC must shift by the same amount, so the gap classification cannot change, assuming no separate change in the other Phillips curve

options.label: B
options.text: The economy must move along its SRPC because the natural rate changed

options.label: C
options.text: Neither Phillips curve changes because the actual data are unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: The LRPC shifts, so the economy's gap classification can change even though its plotted point does not move

options.label: E
options.text: The inflation rate must adjust immediately to keep the economy in long-run equilibrium

explanation: A natural-rate change moves the LRPC horizontally. If the economy's actual point remains fixed, its position relative to the new LRPC can change, changing whether the economy is inflationary, recessionary, or at long-run equilibrium.

prompt: Suppose the SRPC shifts right while the LRPC remains unchanged. Which statement is necessarily true about the new long-run equilibrium point?

options.label: A
options.text: It lies at a higher natural unemployment rate because the SRPC shifted right, with the natural rate otherwise unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: It lies on the same natural unemployment rate but at the intersection of the new SRPC and the unchanged LRPC

options.label: C
options.text: It lies at a lower natural unemployment rate because inflation is higher

options.label: D
options.text: It remains at the old SRPC-LRPC intersection because long-run equilibrium never changes

options.label: E
options.text: It must have zero inflation because the LRPC is unchanged

explanation: With the LRPC unchanged, the natural rate of unemployment is unchanged. The new long-run equilibrium is where the shifted SRPC intersects that same vertical LRPC, potentially at a different inflation rate.

prompt: An economy begins in long-run equilibrium at a 5 percent natural rate. Aggregate demand increases, moving unemployment to 4 percent. An adverse supply shock then shifts the SRPC right while unemployment remains at 4 percent at the instant represented. Which statement is definitely true at that instant?
